newsitem.title: USA: Simpson trial jury selection moves ahead slowly.
newsitem.headline: Simpson trial jury selection moves ahead slowly.

text.p: A black woman who said she was "excited" when O.J. Simpson was acquitted of murder and a white man who said Simpson was "probably guilty" were both retained on Friday for the jury pool in the ex-football star's civil trial.
Of seven potential jurors questioned in the case before the noon lunch break, three were excused because of bias by Judge Hiroshi Fujisaki.

The process of interviewing prospective jurors is going ahead at a snail's pace. After a week, Fujisaki has so far approved only 43 potential jurors for the pool from which 12 jurors and eight alternates will ultimately be selected.
Most of the prospective panellists interviewed have divided along racial lines, with whites generally believing Simpson, who is black, was guilty of killing his white ex-wife and a white friend.
Generally, blacks support the innocent verdict and often express belief in a police conspiracy theory advanced by defence attorneys in last year's criminal trial.

For the third day in row, Simpson was not present in the courthouse where he is being sued by the families of the murder victims. If he is found responsible for the wrongful deaths of Nicole Brown and Ronald Goldman, he could be forced to pay millions of dollars in damages.
One potential juror questioned on Friday, a black woman who appeared to be in her 30s, said under questioning that she had not followed the criminal case closely.
But she remembered finding it "funny" that the glove found at the murder scene and another at Simpson's home appeared not to fit him during a courtroom demonstration.
She described having an emotional reaction to the not-guilty verdicts last Oct. 3.
"I was excited (when the verdicts were read on television)," she said. "I said, 'Oh, he's not guilty'"
Daniel Petrocelli, a lawyer for murder victim Ronald Goldman's father, Fred, asked Fujisaki to remove the woman, but the judge refused, saying he was "satisfied at this point" with her responses.
Also kept on the panel Friday was a white man who appeared to be in his 60s and who said on a jury questionnaire that Simpson was "probably guilty."
The man also felt that the jury in the criminal trial did not spend enough time deliberating and probably did not understand DNA evidence.
But under examination by Simpson's attorney, Robert Baker, the man promised to fairly consider the evidence from both sides and was retained by Fujisaki.

The questioning shows how difficult is to find a jury of people who do not have preconceived opinions about the case as a result of the tremendous media attention paid to the criminal trial, which was televised.
Fujisaki has barred TV cameras from the civil trial and ordered lawyers not to talk about the case in public.
As long as juror candidates do not demonstrate obvious racial prejudice, Fujisaki has tended to accept people who say they can put aside their opinions and consider the case objectively.
In another development Friday, Fred Goldman spoke to reporters outside the courthouse to deny allegations of fraud leveled at his "Ron Goldman Justice Fund".
Goldman said "every penny," except for the costs of sending out letters asking for donations, went toward the fund to help pay lawyers' fees.
He said the fund had received "hundreds of thousands" of dollars in contributions, but that they could not hope to cover the estimated multimillion-dollar costs of the civil case.

Asked about the jury selection process, Goldman, who was very outspoken during the criminal trial, said he could not comment. "I can't address any issues relative to the trial; the gag order prohibits me," he said.
